text:
My ‌first ‌customer ‌paid. The product didn't notice.

What I learned in the weeks after launching a tiny Trello Power-Up

A couple of weeks ago I launched PrimeScheduler, a tiny Trello Power-Up that lets you schedule card comments for a specific time. I wrote about building it last time. This time it's about the thing nobody told you about: what happens after somebody actually pays you for something.

Nothing in here is rocket science. Everything surprised me, nonetheless.

1. "Payment succeeded" and "customer got what they paid for" are two different things

My first paying customer went through checkout. The payment provider was happy. My webhook returned 200 OK. Green all over the place.

The customer still had the free plan.

The payment had no reliable way to be associated with any given user. Somewhere between the website, the checkout process and the webhook, the identity got dropped and my code kindly skipped the event without complaining.

Lesson: the most important line in your billing code is the one that answers "who is this payment for?" Make it impossible to start a checkout without that answer, and make matching a payment to an account an emergency.



2. Silent success is worse than a loud failure

The webhook didn't crash. It returned "ok", logged a line that nobody ever looks at and moved on. From the payment dashboard' point of view, perfect delivery.

If it had thrown an error, the provider would have retried and I would have had some red somewhere.

Lesson: anything that touches money should be loud when it can't do its job. I now get an email when a payment comes in that the system can't associate with an account. Hopefully I'll never get one. The point is that I'll know if I do.



3. Testing the whole purchase is different from testing the parts

I'd tested the checkout. I'd tested the webhook with sample events. I'd never bought my own product, end to end, on a second account, opened the app and checked that the paid features were indeed unlocked.

When I finally did (with a 100% discount code), it broke in a whole new way. A placeholder that I had written in my own notes ended up inside a real link, and the account ID came in with characters it shouldn't have had. Small typo, same result: paid, not upgraded.

Lesson: make a free discount code, have a second test account and run the whole thing after every change to anything near billing. "It works in pieces" means zero.



4. Your logs are already gone before you need them

When I went to investigate, the server logs from the time of the purchase had already expired. That's not uncommon with free hosting tiers, which often have a very short expiration window for logs.

What saved me was the notification history from the payment provider, which keeps the exact payload they sent and the response I sent back. It also let me resend the event once the bug was fixed.

Lesson: know before you need them where the evidence is and how long it stays there. For billing, the event log from the provider is usually the best record you have.



5. Clean-up jobs can quietly take away what people paid for

Most integrations periodically check for users who have disconnected the app so that it can remove their data. Makes sense. Except it also removed their plan. A paying user who disconnected and then reconnected would have lost Pro and still been billed monthly.

Lesson: separate "delete this user's data" from "end this user's subscription." Only the billing system should be able to end a subscription.



6. Your landing page makes promises your code doesn't know about

Reading my own website with fresh eyes, I discovered:

the pricing said "one workspace" while the plan was actually tied to a single person

the free tier, my main entry point, wasn't visible in the hero or the pricing table

a technical limit was sold as a feature of the paid plan

None of these were lies per se. They were things from early drafts that nobody re-read after I changed the product.

Lesson: after launch, read your website as a skeptical customer. Every sentence about pricing should be something your code actually enforces.



7. A face beats a feature list

My first landing page looked like a hundred other AI-generated SaaS pages: dark background, purple glow, emoji labels. It was fine. It was also forgettable, and for a tool that asks for access to your Trello account, forgettable isn't great.

I redesigned it to be more calming and added my photo with a sentence that support emails will go straight to me. For a solo product, "there's a real person behind this" is one of the best trust signals you can make.

8. When something breaks, the first customer deserves a personal email

When I learned that my first customer didn't get what they paid for, I didn't wait for them to complain. I emailed them, told them it was a bug on my side, fixed their account and pushed their next payment back as a thank you for their patience.

It took ten minutes. With one paying customer, that customer is basically your whole business, so treat them like it.

The short version

- Make "who is this payment for?" impossible to get wrong.

- Make billing failures loud.

- Buy your own product, end to end, on a second account.

- Know before you need them where the evidence is and how long it stays there.

- Don't let clean-up code touch subscriptions.

- Re-read your pricing page against your code.

- Put a real person on the page.

- Talk to your first customers personally.

I'm ‌gonna ‌be ‌honest about how the week actually went. First sale was a little big, a few days later I'm looking at a payment I can't attribute to anyone and wondering what else I did wrong. I think that's just what building something alone looks like. No one is reviewing your webhook, or re-reading your pricing page, or calling you out on the clean-up job quietly cancelling people's plans. You discover these things by stumbling onto them.

So if you are in the same place as me, shipping your first paid thing at night after your day job, checking the payment dashboard more often than you'd care to admit, half sure something is wrong: yeah probably something is. That's ok. Mine was, twice in a week. It's fixable, and your first customers will be a lot more forgiving than you think if you just tell them like it is.

I'm actually curious about yours. What broke after your first sale? Leave it in the comments. I think gathering these up is more helpful than another "how I got to 10k MRR" post.

I built a platform with a dozen possible use cases. How do you decide which one to commit to?

I need to pick a lane and I can’t tell which one is right. Here is where I am.

I’m a solo founder, still employed full-time. I built a platform that gives AI assistants structured knowledge to work from. It can serve many use cases, which is the problem. Every one of them looks plausible.

Four lanes I’ve tested, with what actually happened:

1. Individual users (B2C/prosumer). Early adopters found me on Twitter and Reddit. The feedback was good. One person used it heavily during a redesign and left a nice video review. Then nobody came back. Free alternatives (a folder of markdown, a CLAUDE.md) are good enough for one person.

2. Ops and chief-of-staff roles at startups. Pain is real, since knowledge is scattered and decisions aren’t written down. I have a few design partners. Results are mixed: one has no budget, one has access but nobody uses it, one deprioritized it. Cold outreach to this group has stopped yielding after weeks of daily sweeps.

3. A security data use case. I built a hosted lookup for vulnerability and certification data. Existing options mostly need self-hosting and local API keys. It’s the most concrete thing I have, and the buyer is clearly defined. I don’t know yet whether it’s a wedge or a side feature.

4. Education and public data. A UN agency and two universities have shown interest. Slow, budget-dependent, hard to repeat.

My current rule: pick the lane where someone with a budget can say yes within 30 days.

Two questions:

- If you had to bet on one for the next 60 days, which would you pick?

- What evidence would make you drop a lane, and what would make you commit?

I drew the free/paid line at "does it need my server". Now the free tier has to warn people Safari might delete their book

Disclosure up front: I made this. It's NovelDesk, a place to write a novel in the browser. I'm solo, it started as a Mac app, and the web version went live this month.

When I moved it to the web I gave the free version one rule: it never talks to my server. No account, the manuscript sits in the browser's storage, a .docx import gets parsed on your own machine, and a backup is a file you download.

That rule ended up drawing the pricing for me. Anything that needs a server is paid: syncing between devices, keeping every version, Word/EPUB/PDF export, publishing chapters as pages people can read, and the optional AI pictures. Everything else is free, for up to two manuscripts of 30 chapters. Paid is $8 a month or $60 a year.

What I didn't see coming was the storage part. Safari clears a site's data if you don't visit it for 7 days. So the free version can't really promise your book is safe, and I had to say that on the screen. It now says your work is kept for 7 days, and it keeps nudging you to download a backup. It's the least growth-friendly sentence on the whole site and I went back and forth on it for a while. Asking the browser for persistent storage helps on some browsers, but the browser decides, not me.

Two things I'm watching now:

- whether people who hit the 30-chapter limit upgrade or just start a second manuscript

- whether the 7-day warning scares people off before they've written anything

If you run something with a big free tier that only lives on the user's device, how did you explain the "your data is only here" part without making it sound scary?

You don't need 1,000 customers to start testing Product-Market Fit.

You need to ask the right questions to the right customers. 

Sean Ellis popularized a simple PMF test: 

Ask users:
“How would you feel if you could no longer use our product? 

Very disappointed
Somewhat disappointed
Not disappointed 

A result of 40% or more saying “very disappointed” is a useful early signal, not proof of PMF. 

Here's how I'd use it: 

Survey customers who have experienced your products core value.
Ask what they value most.
Identify which customer segment loves the product.
Investigate what's missing for everyone else.
Repeat the survey as the product evolves. 

Don't treat 40% as a universal pass/fail score. 

Combine it with retention, repeat usage and willingness to pay. 

The goal isn't to prove everyone loves your product.
Its to discover who needs it most. 

Seed-stage founders: how many paying customers do you have today? 

Comment with your approximate number.

one person farmed our AI free trial with 9 apple IDs and ran up ~$1,900 in image costs. how do you stop this without punishing real users?

our image generation bill basically tripled in 9 days. installs were flat, revenue didn't move, no launch, no campaign. I spent two evenings staring at dashboards before it occurred to me to just ask.

asked claude to dig through posthog (we log the cost of every generation there) and our subscription data and it found it in a few minutes, screenshot is that chat: a single device made 14,178 generations since oct 6, more than all our other users combined. it started 9 free trials from 9 different apple IDs, cancelled each one before it converted, never paid a cent.

our trial limit was checked per account, not per device. so every new apple id = a fresh 3 day trial with unlimited generations.

we're adding a per-device cap now, but a lot of real families share one ipad and I don't want to block them. per device, per payment method, a daily generation limit during the trial... what has actually worked for you without annoying normal users?

text:
Am I solving a real problem, or is this just another tool nobody needs?

I've been thinking about something that keeps happening whenever I work with different AI tools.

Let's say you've spent hours working on a project in ChatGPT or Claude. The AI already understands your idea, requirements, decisions, and where you're headed.

Then you switch to another AI tool, maybe Codex for development or Higgsfield for generating visuals.

Suddenly, you're starting from scratch. You have to explain the project again, rewrite prompts, and hope the new AI understands everything correctly.

Sure, you can copy-paste conversations, but that gets messy, especially with larger projects.

So I'm exploring an idea called Contexfer.

The concept is pretty simple: Your context should move with you, even when you switch AI tools.

Imagine being able to:

- Transfer project context from one AI model to another without starting over.

- Move conversations between AI assistants or agents.

- Preserve important decisions, requirements, and project progress.

- Generate structured context that another AI can understand without reading hundreds of messages.

The idea isn't to build another chatbot. It's to create a bridge between the AI tools we already use.

We're still exploring the concept, and before spending months building something, I'd rather find out whether this is a problem people actually experience.

A few questions:

- Have you ever struggled to transfer context between AI tools?

- How do you currently handle it? Copy-paste, Markdown files, custom prompts, or something else?

- Would you genuinely use a tool like this, or do existing solutions already work well enough?

And if you think this is a terrible idea, I'd actually love to hear why.

I'm not trying to sell anything. Just trying to figure out whether this problem is worth solving before going too deep into development.

Curious to hear your experiences.

Detecting Grok Bot on your website.

I was testing Grok's browser environment through test.leonix.io, and something interesting happened. Grok went from looking like a browser running in a cloud environment to something much closer to a regular desktop browser.

Grok: Before vs. Now

Signal Previous Grok Latest Grok             Browser Chrome 154 Chrome 155   Operating system Linux Linux   IP provider Cloudflare Verizon Business   Network type Hosting ISP   Datacenter detected Yes No   VPN detected Yes No   Relay detected Yes No   Virtual machine detected Yes No   GPU renderer SwiftShader (Subzero) Intel UHD Graphics 630   Logical processors 8 8   Device memory 16 GB 16 GB   Screen resolution 1920 × 1200 1920 × 1200   1. SwiftShader is gone

Previously, Grok exposed SwiftShader (Subzero), a software based GPU renderer commonly found in virtualized or cloud browser environments. Now it reports Intel UHD Graphics 630, using Mesa and OpenGL. This doesn't necessarily mean it's running on physical hardware, but it removes one of the more obvious clues we previously observed.

2. The network looks completely different

Few days back, Grok traffic came through Cloudflare and was classified as datacenter traffic. VPN and relay detection were also positive. Now the connection comes through Verizon Business, classified as an ISP. No datacenter flag. No VPN flag. No relay flag. That's quite a change for anyone relying on network intelligence to identify automated browsers.

So what does this tell us?

A few days ago, identifying this Grok session using infrastructure and browser signals looked relatively straightforward. Now those signals have disappeared. It doesn't prove Grok deliberately changed its environment to avoid detection.

And for those relying on HTTP headers to detect Grok, the identifying header we previously observed has been absent from our tests since October 9. If your agent detection depends on a header, an IP range, or SwiftShader, what happens when all three disappear? Grok is trying its best to look like human, would love to hear what you all found. If you're dealing with unwanted AI agent traffic and looking for a lightweight, low-code way to detect it, feel free to reach out.

text:
421 users. Only 5 sales. And a big lesson about SaaS customer acquisition.

I recently reached 421 users on my SaaS, but only 5 of them actually paid.

And it made me think about something a lot of founders seem to overlook.
User numbers mean absolutely nothing if nobody is willing to pay for your product.
I’ve noticed that many SaaS founders tend to believe that the best acquisition strategy is to attract as many users as possible.

The logic is pretty simple:

“If I can get 10,000 users, even if only 2% pay, that’s still 200 paying customers!”

Sounds great in theory. But in practice, it doesn’t always work that way.
With the explosion of new SaaS products, a lot of people sign up simply out of curiosity, to try something new, or just to use the free version.

And if your product doesn’t provide enough value, why would they pay?
The real issue is CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost).

Imagine spending $1,000 to acquire 500 users, but only 5 become paying customers.

Your cost per signup is $2, but your actual CAC is $200 per paying customer.

And even if you manage to convert some users, if they don’t find enough value in your product, you’re likely to face a high churn rate.

Personally, I’d rather attract 50 people who genuinely need what my product offers than 5,000 curious users who just want to try the latest SaaS tool.

Signups feed your ego. Paying customers keep your SaaS alive. And retention proves its value.

What do you think? As a founder, do you prioritize user volume or more targeted customer acquisition?
